_comment: Readings taken off the manufacturer's reference calculator. This is the ONLY
check in dev/replay.mjs that can confirm accuracy rather than self-consistency.
The original ~43 readings behind the Duplex constants were never stored - they
survive only as prose in the source comments, and that prose has drifted: the
0.2625/0.2253 note still quotes x = 15.597 / 15.265, which no drum reproduces
with the C the code now holds. The underlying readings were recoverable in that
one case because the note also gave the resulting lengths, which bracket C. Most
notes do not, and those readings are gone.
status 'verified' - full inputs and expected outputs; replay.mjs asserts it.
status 'partial'  - recorded from a comment but missing inputs (usually the
drum). NOT asserted. This is the re-measurement worklist.
Add readings with: node dev/worklist.mjs   (see dev/README.md)

readings.source: Reference calculator API response, supplied by the user 2026-10-01. Inputs pinned by the returned multiplier and TIPPT.
note: LENGTH CONFIRMS THE CATALOG FORMULA. active = 1 x 2463.10 / 136.7855 =
18.005 -> 18, with no fitted constant. The old fitted C gave 18.4507 and
the old rule then added 0.25", for 18.25".
The reference's own spring weights confirm the lengths independently:
STEEL_DENSITY x (pi^2/4) x wire x (ID + wire) x L reproduces 13.2669 and
26.8447 to four decimals at L = 18 and 19 exactly.
referenceCycles is recorded but NOT asserted: the duplex cycle model is
still unresolved. Inverting the reference's own counts needs 3-5% more
inner-spring torque than the physical active length produces, and no
single factor reconciles all six readings (the implied ratio runs 1.003
to 1.056). The field is confirmed to be computed life, not the target
echoed back: 585 lb returns 12,000 against a 10,000 target.

note: NOW REPRODUCED by the long-active regime - see the 405-438 lb sweep on this
same rung, which showed the bonus is a constant +2.25 there.
THE ONE READING THE PHYSICAL FORMULA DOES NOT REPRODUCE, and the only one
with a fractional length. Marked 'divergent' so replay.mjs records it
without asserting it.
The reference REJECTS this design itself: status 'warning', 'cycle life
calculation of 1,165,000.00 exceeds the 350,000 cycle maximum'.
It also contradicts itself here. Inverting its own reported cycle count
gives a body length of 34.773, which agrees with the catalog formula's
34.875 to 0.3% - while it prints 36.25. So its internal arithmetic uses
the same active length everything else does, and only the PRINTED length
differs. Until that is understood, fitting the general rule to this
reading is what produced the tau regime in the first place.
Both wires are also at or near their minimum for their spring ID (0.2253
is exactly the published minimum for 3 3/4"), so the design is pinned at
the soft end of the ladder and cannot step down.

readings.source: Comment on the 0.2730/0.2253 entry: 'Two readings (600 lb at 7'0", 572 lb at 11'2")'. Drum, spring count, radius and target not recorded, and no length given, so nothing can be asserted.
Comment on the 0.2830/0.2343 entry: three readings at 683 lb, at 11'2", 11'0" and 9'0", used to pin tau to 20.25-21.25. Lengths not recorded.

Comment on the 0.2890/0.2343 entry: the 726/727 lb pair either side of the reference's own accept/reject line at 11'0", which brackets K to within 4. The most valuable reading type described anywhere in the file - a boundary - and the inputs behind it were not kept.
Reference calculator API response, supplied by the user 2026-10-01.
note: NOW REPRODUCED. This reading was marked divergent while the quarter inch was
unexplained. With the three-regime thresholds fitted from this rung's own
9-point sweep it comes out exactly, length and weights.
THE QUARTER INCH IS REAL, and this reading proves it. 16.25", straight
from the API, on an in-range design the reference does not complain about.
It also vindicates the old source comment, which claimed exactly 16.25" at
460 lb and 15.00" at 470 lb. That comment was briefly marked superseded
here on the grounds that its quoted x values no longer reproduced - the x
values were stale, but the LENGTHS it reported were right.
WHAT THE FORMULA GIVES: active = 2 x 1014.75 / 133.875 = 15.158, which
rounds to 15. The reference says 16.25, so this is +1.09 out.
THE 460/470 PAIR IS THE SHARPEST EVIDENCE IN THE FILE. Same drum, same
height, same spring count, same wires, 10 lb apart - and the reference
steps 16.25" -> 15", a drop of 1.25", where the active length moves only
0.32". That is a genuine quantisation, not rounding, and no smooth
function of the active length reproduces it.
Both quarter-inch readings so far (this and 200 lb) are on the SOFTEST
pairing, 0.2625/0.2253, where the inner wire sits exactly at its
published minimum for 3 3/4" and cannot step down.

readings.source: Reference calculator API response, supplied by the user 2026-10-01, as part of a TARGET SWEEP on one door: 470 lb, 1 spring, 7'0", D400-144, radius 15. TIPPT 136.8 and turns 7.9 are identical across the whole sweep, so only the target varies - which is what makes these the cleanest available test of the cycle model.
note: FOUR NEW PAIRINGS came out of this sweep - 0.3625/0.289, 0.3938/0.3065,
0.3938/0.3195 and 0.4062/0.331 - none of them in DUPLEX_PAIRS. All four fall
inside duplexPairBalanced's stress window, which is independent confirmation
of that rule: 7 of 7 sweep pairings are in the window.
IT ALSO CONTRADICTS DUPLEX_CATALOGUE, which claims a 50,000 target tops out
at S = 5920. The reference used S = 8723 at exactly that target. Since S
depends only on the two wire sizes, a product catalogue cannot depend on
spring count - yet at 2 springs the cap makes this very pairing unreachable.

readings.source: Reference calculator API response, user-supplied 2026-10-01. Part of a DENSE WEIGHT SWEEP: 440-480 lb in 5 lb steps, 2 springs, 7'0", D400-144, radius 15, target 10,000. One pairing (0.2625/0.2253) throughout, so only the active length varies - the cleanest test of the length rule anywhere in this file.
note: THE SWEEP IS NON-MONOTONIC IN WEIGHT, which is the whole finding:
wt   TIPPT   active    frac    reference L
A HEAVIER DOOR GETS A LONGER SPRING at 445->450 and again at 475->480. No
monotonic function of the active length can do that, so the quarter inch is
a genuine quantisation and not rounding.
ON THIS PAIRING the rule that fits all nine is:
frac(active) ~ 0        ->  L = round(active)
0.01 < frac < ~0.6      ->  L = ceil(active) + 0.25
frac > ~0.6             ->  L = ceil(active)
tau bracketed between frac 0.5290 (gets the quarter) and 0.6734 (does not).
BUT IT DOES NOT GENERALISE, and that is why it is not implemented. Six
readings on OTHER pairings have frac in the 0.01-0.6 band and take NO
those plain round(active) is exact. So the quarter belongs to this pairing,
or to something about it not yet identified - note it is the SOFTEST rung on
the ladder, and the out-of-range 200 lb anomaly is on it too.
Implementing an unexplained per-pairing regime is exactly what produced the
tau constant that this work removed, and tau is why no drum but the D400-144
ever came out right. Characterised here rather than coded.

note: Two new pairings, 0.289/0.2343 and 0.3065/0.2437, neither in DUPLEX_PAIRS.
Both inside duplexPairBalanced's window.
These two are at 21" and 27" - BELOW the 34" ceiling - and the length rule
is exact on both. Together with the 1-spring arm failing at 40"+ on the

readings.source: Reference API, user-supplied 2026-10-01. Taken to test a predicted 15.25" at 680/685 lb; the prediction turned out to be for the wrong rung (see note).
note: THE 90% ACCEPTANCE RULE - the most important thing these three readings show.
680 lb returns 10,000 on 0.283/0.2343 and 685 lb returns 9,000 on the SAME
rung with status 'warning'. At 690 lb it steps to 0.289/0.2343. That is the
second such boundary: 725 lb does exactly the same on 0.289/0.2343 before
stepping to 0.295 at 730.
Both boundaries sit at 9,000 against a 10,000 target - exactly 0.90. So the
reference accepts the softest rung reaching about 90% of target and WARNS
below 100%, rather than requiring the target outright. That is the behaviour
the source comments have described since the first commit as 'takes a
combination that does not reach the target'.
CONFIRMED A THIRD WAY, from the reference's own data and with no reliance on
this app's K: 620 lb measures 14,000 cycles on 0.283/0.2253. Scaling to 680
lb by the cycle law alone, 14,000 / (680/620)^4.67 = 9,000 - right on the
boundary. So at 680 lb that rung falls to 90% and the reference steps off it,
which is precisely what it does.
WHY THE RULE IS NOT IMPLEMENTED. Scored over 27 readings, loosening the
threshold makes the wire choice WORSE, not better:
The rule is right and the model still gets worse with it, because a lower
threshold lets MORE rungs qualify and so amplifies every error in K. At 680
lb this app thinks 0.283/0.2253 still clears the target when the reference's
own numbers put it at 9,000. The strict f = 1.00 currently in use is
compensating for optimistic K values.
That makes three compensating errors now identified - the strict threshold,
DUPLEX_CATALOGUE's cap, and the pessimistic kSlope line - each of which
measures worse when fixed alone. K has to be fixed first.

note: THE 90% ACCEPTANCE RULE - the most important thing these three readings show.
680 lb returns 10,000 on 0.283/0.2343 and 685 lb returns 9,000 on the SAME
rung with status 'warning'. At 690 lb it steps to 0.289/0.2343. That is the

reference accepts the softest rung reaching about 90% of target and WARNS
below 100%, rather than requiring the target outright. That is the behaviour

combination that does not reach the target'.

boundary. So at 680 lb that rung falls to 90% and the reference steps off it,
which is precisely what it does.

compensating for optimistic K values.

readings.source: Reference API, user-supplied 2026-10-01 from live testing. FIRST 3-SPRING reading and FIRST LHR-radius reading in this file. Reference returned status 'error' with two messages: the torsion assembly is too long for a 108" door, and the 602,000 cycle life exceeds the 350,000 maximum.
note: NOW REPRODUCED by the long-active regime - see the 405-438 lb sweep on this
same rung, which showed the bonus is a constant +2.25 there.
IT ALSO CAUGHT TWO WARNING BUGS, both now fixed.
The reference returned "Torsion assembly will be too long for a 108 \" wide
door!" and this app said nothing: assemblyLengthExact was built from the
SINGLE spring length and the Wire Size dropdown, giving 98.86" against a real
126.33". It now uses the Duplex outer spring and the warning fires.
The message text was wrong too. A note in the source claimed the reference
printed the ASSEMBLY LENGTH into that sentence; this reading shows it prints
the DOOR WIDTH, 108. Corrected, spacing and all.
WHAT THIS READING VERIFIES, and it is a lot:
multiplier   0.285354 exact to 6 decimals - the LHR track-radius curve had
never been tested on a Duplex reading before
turns        8.0369, matching the reference's implied value
TIPPT        99.303 against its 99.3
wire         0.2625/0.2253, correct - the first 3-SPRING selection tested
So the LHR curve, the 3-spring scaling and the wire ladder are all right here.
WHAT IT DOES NOT: the length. active = 3 x 1014.85 / 99.303 = 30.659, and the
reference says 32.25 - a bonus of +2.25 over the floor, which none of the
three regimes can produce (they give +0, +1.25 or +1).
IT ALSO CORRECTS AN EARLIER CLAIM in this file that the length rule was exact
under 34". It is not. Ordered by active length the failures now run 30.66,
34.87, 46.19 while 31.89 and 33.94 pass, so the breakage is not a function of
length at all and the 'long spring' framing was wrong.
TWO READINGS NOW NEED +2.25 - this one and the 200 lb case. Both are on the
softest rung, 0.2625/0.2253, and both are over the reference's own 350,000
cycle maximum, which it reports as an error. That may be the pattern or may be
coincidence; two readings cannot say. A third over-max case on a different
rung would settle it.

readings.source: Reference API, user-supplied 2026-10-01. Designed probe: same rung, drum, radius, height and target as the two +2.25 readings, varying ONLY frac(active) - 0.020 here against their 0.871 and 0.659.
note: THIS KILLS THE 'OVER-MAX MEANS +2.25' HYPOTHESIS, and the model was right.
The reference returns 35.25", which is floor(34.020) + 1.25 - the ordinary
quarter-inch regime - not the +2.25 that the 200 lb and 348 lb readings show.
This case is over the 350,000 maximum too (1,042,000 cycles, reported as a
warning), so being over-max is NOT what produces +2.25.
It also VALIDATES the fitted thresholds well outside the range they came
from: tLo/tHi for this rung were fitted on a 440-480 lb sweep where active
runs 14.5-15.8, and they are correct here at active 34.020. So for this rung
they transfer across more than a doubling of length.

readings.source: Reference API, user-supplied 2026-10-01. Designed probe: the shortest over-max design reachable on a rung other than the softest, which needs a 300,000 target.
note: THIS FALSIFIES THE THREE-REGIME LENGTH MODEL, and the proof is short.
On this rung, 0.273/0.2253:
580 lb   active 13.513   frac 0.513   reference bonus +0.00
286 lb   active 27.404   frac 0.404   reference bonus +1.25
frac 0.513 requires tLo > 0.513. frac 0.404 requires tLo <= 0.404. No
threshold on frac(active) satisfies both, so the length cannot be a function
of frac(active) and a per-rung threshold pair alone.
WHAT SEPARATES THEM is the integer part: 13 against 27. The thresholds for
this rung were fitted on a 560-600 lb sweep where active stays near 13.5, and
they are wrong at 27.4. Note the contrast with the 205 lb reading above,
where the other rung's thresholds DID transfer from active ~15 to ~34. So
the transfer is not reliable, and frac(active) is evidently a coordinate that
only correlates locally with whatever the reference actually quantises.
NOT PATCHED. The thresholds stay as fitted because they are right on 47 of
48 readings; this one is recorded as the counterexample that says the model
is locally valid rather than correct. Fixing it needs a sweep at a second
integer part of active on the same rung - weights around 270-300 lb at a
300,000 target would walk frac across its range near active 27.
RESOLVED 2026-10-02. Was divergent; now reproduced exactly, including the 28.25 quarter inch at 2 springs.

readings.source: Reference API, user-supplied 2026-10-01. DENSE SWEEP AT LONG ACTIVE LENGTH: 405-438 lb, 3 springs, radius 12, 11'6", on the 0.2625/0.2253 rung. Taken to settle the +2.25 bonus after three separate hypotheses for it had been falsified. Also the first radius-12 and first 11'6" readings in the file. Every one returns status 'error' - the assembly is too long for a 108" door, which the app now reports too.
note: THIS SETTLED THE +2.25 BONUS.
wt   active   frac    refL    refL - floor
Every reading is exactly floor(active) + 2.25, across frac 0.110 to 0.798 -
a CONSTANT bonus with no threshold anywhere inside that span. With the other
long readings on this rung that makes 10 of 11 at +2.25, the lone exception
being frac 0.020 which takes +1.25, so the split lies between 0.020 and 0.110.
WHAT IT MEANS. The rung's thresholds depend on the ACTIVE LENGTH as well as
the rung. Short range, 9 readings at active 14.5-15.8: split between 0.529
and 0.673, upper band +1. Long range, 11 readings at active 30.7-38.2: split
between 0.020 and 0.110, upper band +2.25. Same shape, different numbers.
That is exactly what the 286 lb counterexample had already implied when it
showed no single frac threshold could serve one rung at two integer parts of
active. This is the positive version of that finding.
STILL GUESSED: where one range ends and the other begins. Active 15.8 to 30.7
is unsampled, so any boundary in that gap fits equally well; 23 is its
midpoint. Three readings between active 18 and 28 would pin it.

the rung. Short range, 9 readings at active 14.5-15.8: split between 0.529
and 0.673, upper band +1. Long range, 11 readings at active 30.7-38.2: split
between 0.020 and 0.110, upper band +2.25. Same shape, different numbers.
That is exactly what the 286 lb counterexample had already implied when it
showed no single frac threshold could serve one rung at two integer parts of
active. This is the positive version of that finding.
STILL GUESSED: where one range ends and the other begins. Active 15.8 to 30.7
is unsampled, so any boundary in that gap fits equally well; 23 is its
midpoint. Three readings between active 18 and 28 would pin it.

readings.source: Reference API, user-supplied 2026-10-02. FIRST HI-LIFT Duplex reading, FIRST 4-SPRING reading, and the heaviest door in the file at 1062 lb. D800-120 with 72" of hi-lift, 16'0" high, 14'2" wide.
note: WHAT THIS VERIFIES, and it is the broadest single reading in the file:
the HI-LIFT path on Duplex, never tested before - turns 11.0870 against the
reference's 11.1, TIPPT 471.100 against 471.1
FOUR SPRINGS, never tested before - the wire choice 0.3437/0.273 is correct,
so the spring-count scaling holds at 4 as well as 1, 2 and 3
a 1062 lb door, nearly half again the heaviest previously read
THE MULTIPLIER IS 1.4e-05 OUT: 0.443597 against 0.443611. That is the
documented hi-lift interpolation error, not a new fault - the HL800 note puts
between-column error at 4.3e-05 median and 2.1e-04 worst, and 72" sits
between measured columns. It is harmless here because TIPPT still rounds to
the same 471.1, but near a length rounding boundary it would not be.
THE LENGTH IS 0.25" SHORT, and it is a new failure mode rather than one of
the known ones:
active 28.294, reference 28.25, so the bonus is +0.25 - a value no other
reading has produced. The known bonuses are 0, +1, +1.25 and +2.25.
it is also the FIRST reading where the reference length is BELOW the active
length. Every other one of the 70 is above it, by +1 to +2.25.
THE RUNG NOW HAS TWO READINGS THAT DISAGREE on the rounding:
470 lb  1 spring  D400-144 standard  t25,000  active 24.368 -> 24      +0.00
Three things differ between them - spring count, drum family and hi-lift - so
two readings cannot say which matters. The discriminator is the same rung at
4 springs on a STANDARD drum: if it rounds like the hi-lift case the cause is
the spring count, if like the 470 lb case it is the drum. On the D525-216 that
is roughly 1200 lb, 4 springs, 8'0", target 50,000, which lands at active
25.436 - floor would give 25, the +0.25 rule 25.25.
NOT PATCHED on one reading.

RESOLVED 2026-10-02. Was divergent because the +0.25 bonus appeared in no other reading and the rung's two readings disagreed on the rounding. Both questions are now answered, and NOT by a special case: the bonus is produced by the 4-spring band derived for this rung from the hi-lift sweeps (batches 5-7, 131 distinct hi-lift readings), and the disagreement with the 470 lb 1-spring reading was simply the spring count - the bands are keyed on (rung, spring count), so the two readings live in different groups and never had to agree. The multiplier is still 1.4e-05 out, which remains harmless here.

Reference calculator, automated pull 2026-10-05 (batch q1, 363 cases). Two contiguous 5 lb weight ladders on the D525-216 at 25,000 cycles, 96in, radius 15 - one at two springs and one at one spring, 300-1100 lb - plus a 41-reading 1 lb window at two springs around 738 lb. Taken to bracket a LENGTH step inside a single rung, which no previous batch could do: the dense 1 lb sweeps were all aimed at rung switches, where the length does not move. These ladders walk about 35 rungs and produce 59 within-rung length steps. They are what showed the bonus sorting monotonically by frac on 0.2625/0.2253, and they are also the first readings to show the length rising with weight inside a rung.

Reference calculator, automated pull 2026-10-05 (batch F2, 340 cases, 339 clean). WALKS THE FRACTION rather than the weight. The quarter-inch bonus is a function of frac(active length), and a weight ladder mostly cannot see it: of 49 groups in batch q2, 42 held only whole lengths. This batch picks weights so frac is covered uniformly in twentieths across the six (rung, spring count) groups that carried 20 of the 32 remaining clean misses - the soft end at two springs, which is also the most common configuration there is. Every sample comes from a DIFFERENT configuration (drum, radius, cycle target, height), so frac is covered without the batch becoming a line through the input space, which is what cost 2 points when q2 was folded in. Orderable doors only: a first attempt scanned weight upward and took the first match, landing on springs so over-engineered the reference returned 4.6 million cycles and a warning, so the generator now requires our own warning set to be empty - 12,712 flagged candidates rejected. It makes the rule visible for the first time: on 0.2625/0.2253 at three springs a single threshold, bonus 0.25 below frac 0.745 and 1.25 above, explains all 60 readings.

Reference calculator, automated pull 2026-10-06 (batch U1), part of the first UNIFORM corpus. Drawn with dev/eval-sample.mjs over the whole allowed box - six drums, all radii, 1-4 springs, ten cycle targets, height and weight uniform inside each drum's own rating, hi-lift where the drum supports it - rather than targeted at switch points or thresholds like everything before it. The point is to fit the distribution the model is SCORED on: in sample it was 99 percent and on a fresh uniform draw 91, and the corpus being mostly targeted batches is the likeliest cause of that gap. Flagged readings carry flagged:true, so their pairing and cycle count are fitted and their length is not.
